wine.name: Steiner Kékfrankos
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos alone, the grape Austria calls Blaufränkisch.
wine.sites: The Steiner vineyard of Balf, called Spern Steiner when the family bought it in 1997: a slope where gneiss and mica schist reach the surface, leaving a porous, stony ground that stays dry and warm.
wine.making: By the house's notes for the 2018 vintage, the grapes fermented with their own yeasts for about two weeks in wooden or concrete vats, went through malolactic fermentation naturally and then aged for two years in 500 litre barrels. The house has made its Balf wines without additives since 2000.
wine.glass: Black and sour cherry with damson plum, white pepper and clove over a stony, iron edge; fresh acidity carries a firm, fine grained tannin to a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release after its two years in barrel, it gains depth over five to ten years from the vintage in a good year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Weninger's Steiner is a single vineyard Kékfrankos from Balf, outside Sopron, where gneiss and mica schist break the surface: dark cherry, white pepper and a stony grip, from a family that grows Blaufränkisch across the border in Burgenland too. Serve it a little cool.
records.story: The Weninger family grows Blaufränkisch in Austria's Burgenland, which belonged to Hungary until 1921, when that land passed to Austria and a plebiscite kept Sopron and its villages Hungarian. The family first crossed the border in 1992, founding a winery in southern Hungary with a Villány grower, and in 1997 it bought a second Hungarian estate at Balf, just outside Sopron. Among its vines was a slope then called Spern Steiner, planted mostly with Kékfrankos. As the house tells it, the Sopron archive shows the site once grew mainly Furmint for a sweet Ödenburger Ausbruch, Ödenburg being Sopron's German name, and the town chronicles of 1680 prized it above the other vineyards of western Hungary; after phylloxera, red grapes and Kékfrankos took its place. The founders' son has run Balf since 2000, the year the house gave up additives for spontaneous fermentation, and the family joined the Respekt group of biodynamic growers in 2006. Steiner is the wine that carries that history: one named vineyard and one grape, made without additives. For a sommelier it is the bridge across the border, the same grape and the same family on both sides of a line drawn in 1921.

wine.grapes: Kékfrankos alone, the grape Austria calls Blaufränkisch.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards near Sopron, bought back in 1993; the house names no single vineyard for this wine.

records.table: Pfneiszl's Újra Együtt, Together Again, is a Sopron Kékfrankos from a family that left its vineyards for Austria and bought land back in 1993: sour cherry, pink pepper and bright acidity. Pour it a little cool with roast pork or game.
records.story: The Pfneiszl family grew vines around Sopron before the communist years, when, as the family tells it, the grandparents left their vineyards and crossed into Austria. There the name lost its z and became Pfneisl, the spelling the family's Austrian wines carry. After the fall of communism Hungary compensated those whose property had been taken, and in 1993 the sisters' father used restitution vouchers to buy land around Sopron again, founding the estate under the old Hungarian spelling. For its first years it was run from Austria by the father and his brothers. In 2006 two sisters of the next generation, raised in Austria, took the Sopron estate on and made it their own, with a range of Kékfrankos and red cuvées. Újra Együtt, Together Again, is the wine that tells that story on its label: a nod, by the family's account, to its reunion with the vineyards the grandparents had left. It is a Sopron Kékfrankos of sour cherry and pepper, drawn from the district's own grape. For a sommelier it is the human side of a border district: a family split by the Iron Curtain, a vineyard bought back, and a wine named for coming home.

report: The plan's doubt: Offbeat Budapest calls Újra Együtt the lighter, juicier of the family's Kékfrankos, yet the house's own page gives a recent vintage a long rest in barrique (22 months in the summary read); the record keeps barrel ageing, gives no figure and keeps juicy in the glass, and a checker who can read the house's sheet should settle it.
No source says outright which Kékfrankos the house leads with; Újra Együtt is the one critics and importers abroad list most often, and its story is the house's own, so the pick stands.

Left out for want of a second source: the village in Burgenland where the grandparents settled (one account), the estate's organic methods (one merchant), its soils (Offbeat Budapest says limestone and slate, another listing volcanic), and a critic's note that the wine comes from a young vineyard.
The grandparents' flight is told as the family's account; no source gives its year, so the story says the communist years.
The father, his brothers and the two sisters are living and are not named.

wine.name: Chardonnay Brut
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, a blanc de blancs.
wine.sites: The Kogl vineyard, by the house's account the coolest of the family's sites near Sopron, gives the base wine.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, with its second fermentation and its ageing on the lees in the bottle. By the house's own account the family makes the base wine and the Szigeti sparkling wine house at Gols, across the border in Burgenland, turns it into sparkling wine to the family's design. The time on the lees is not published.
wine.glass: Ripe apple and lemon over brioche, with honey and a touch of spice from its time on the lees; golden in colour, with fine, lasting bubbles and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Ready on release; drink it within a few years, while the apple and lemon are fresh and the brioche has not yet turned to honey.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a narrow flute.

records.table: Taschner's Chardonnay Brut is a Sopron blanc de blancs made by the traditional method: Chardonnay from the family's cool Kogl vineyard, given its second fermentation in bottle by a sparkling house at Gols, across the border. Apple, lemon and brioche; pour it as an aperitif.
records.story: Sopron is a town of red wine, and Taschner is a house of whites and sparkling wine as well as reds. The family's roots in wine go back to its grandparents' wine tavern in the town, and by the house's own account it has built the estate since 1995, as a family business growing step by step. In 2004 it built its present winehouse on the hillside known as Pihenőkereszt, looking over the town towards the Schneeberg in Austria. The house grows the district's Kékfrankos and Zweigelt beside its whites, and it grows the classic grapes of Champagne for sparkling wine, made by the traditional method. Its Chardonnay Brut is a blanc de blancs: the base wine comes from the Kogl vineyard, the coolest of its sites, and the second fermentation in bottle is carried out to the family's design by the Szigeti sparkling wine house at Gols, on the far side of the lake. The arrangement suits a border district, where the same climate and the same grapes run on both sides. The house's Fidelissima cuvées share their name with Sopron's Latin title, Civitas Fidelissima, given for its loyalty in the plebiscite of 1921. For a sommelier, the Chardonnay Brut answers a guest who asks for a Hungarian sparkling wine made as Champagne is made.

records.table: Luka's Pinot Noir comes from a small family cellar at Fertőrákos, in the hills between the village and Balf above Lake Fertő: wild strawberry and ripe cherry with velvety tannin, fermented with its own yeasts and rested in used barrels. Serve it cool, beside duck or trout.
records.story: Fertőrákos sits on the Hungarian shore of the lake the Hungarians call Fertő and the Austrians Neusiedlersee. In December 1921 Sopron and its villages voted in a plebiscite to stay Hungarian, while the land to the north and west went to Austria, and the lake has been shared by two countries since. Luka is a small family winery in the hills between Fertőrákos and Balf; Magyar Bor's directory gives its founding as 2002. Its founder died suddenly, and his daughter left her earlier career to carry on what he had begun, as she told Magyar Bor more than twenty years later. He had favoured Zweigelt; she counts Kékfrankos the pride of Sopron and a priority of the house, and Magyar Bor names Luka among the houses that make a dedicated Kékfrankos from the Steiner vineyard. Pinot Noir grows well on these slopes beside Kékfrankos, Zweigelt and Furmint, and Luka's is a light, fragrant red, fermented with its own yeasts and rested in used barrels. For a sommelier its Pinot Noir is the lakeside cool of Sopron in a glass, and a reminder that the district's reds are not Kékfrankos alone.

records.table: Ráspi's Kékfrankos comes from a chef's winery in the family farmhouse on the main street of Fertőrákos, by Lake Fertő: blackberry, dark cherry and black pepper with firm tannin, from a bare, chalky vineyard of the village. Pour it with the kitchen's game.
records.story: Fertőrákos is a lakeside village north of Sopron, on the Hungarian shore of Lake Fertő. Ráspi is the house of a chef and winemaker who grew up in the family farmhouse on the village's main street, and both the restaurant and the winery work from it. The name is a nickname. As the family tells it, it was first given to the chef's father, who sharpened his scythe with a rasp, ráspoly in Hungarian, at the winter reed harvests on the lake, and it stands on the wine labels and over the restaurant door. The restaurant opened in 1994, a small room with a short menu built on the seasons and on the family's garden. In 2003, by the house's account, the son took over the family winery, and its vineyards on the Újhegy and the Kereszthegy of the village grew from there. Sopron is the home of Kékfrankos, and Magyar Bor names Ráspi among the houses that make a dedicated wine from one site: its Kékfrankos from a bare, chalky vineyard of Fertőrákos. For a sommelier, Ráspi is the place where Sopron's food and wine meet at one table, in a farmhouse by the lake.
